A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiffMJX and Contacts From Distance research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite the revised title and extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original gradient-quality simulations, parameter estimation using Contactnets data, and musculoskeletal MPC experiments, including supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds cube-reorientation experiments and a diagnostic experiment with 20 parallel simulations.

M1.justification: Adaptive integration, collision smoothing, CFD contact forces, and backward-only straight-through gradients are retained. The adjoint alternatives already appear in v1 Appendix B. v2 documents collision and muscle-gradient fixes more explicitly, without establishing a revision to the underlying procedure.

E1.justification: Section 5.2 adds cube reorientation both in the hand and on a surface. This substantially extends MPC coverage from ball-positioning tasks to simultaneous position and orientation control under different contact conditions. Contactnets and the earlier simulation and manipulation tasks remain.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same MJX/DiffMJX and CFD variants, fixed/adaptive integrators, and predictive-sampling comparators with 64, 256, or 1024 samples. The new cube tasks extend the existing MPC comparator set; newly cited planning research does not introduce an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The new cube tasks combine position error with squared quaternion-orientation error. Figure 20 adds a protocol using 20 different initial ball heights, disabled gravity, and per-environment timestep measurements. Existing parameter-identification settings and MPC planning, optimization, and execution budgets are unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 20 adds a targeted analysis of independent adaptive timestep selection during batched execution. The cube tasks also extend CFD-on/off analysis to different contact conditions. The integrator benchmark and billiard adjoint-method comparison already existed in v1 Figures S6 and S3.

E5.justification: Neither version provides seeded replication counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the main comparisons. Existing parameter-initialization trajectories remain. The 20 distinct-height environments in v2 constitute a diagnostic design, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Figure 14 adds substantial MPC results: gradient methods solve in-hand cube reorientation, while CFD is needed to satisfy both position and orientation objectives on the surface. Figure 20 adds timestep trajectories requiring 36–51 solver steps. Earlier fitting results and MPC curves are retained; Figure 12 changes Figure 10's styling, not its values.

T1.justification: New Appendix C.3 invokes order-p discrete-adjoint consistency and tolerance-based state/sensitivity error scaling under Lipschitz and stability conditions. This adds mathematical justification through cited results, rather than a new proof. The existing adjoint and straight-through equations are retained or relocated.

C1.justification: The central claims about accurate hard-contact gradients and informative backward-only CFD gradients remain. v2's introduction adds an explicit, qualified novelty claim that adaptive integration's utility for differentiable simulation had not previously been explored.

C2.justification: v2 adds discussion of contact velocity, batching slowdowns, low-dimensional finite-difference alternatives, unsupported mesh collisions, and the cube tasks' contact mechanisms. Most earlier limitations move to Appendices B/D. However, v1's explicit system-identification warning about local minima, pre-tuned contact parameters, and possible global optimization is omitted.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 substantially expands reproducibility information through named collision pairs, sigmoid interpolation, plane-box collision code, and muscle-wrapping gradient remedies. Appendix B adds concrete checkpoint and solver-budget guidance. The project link changes from a website to a repository; existing experimental hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain.

R1.justification: v2 expands its comparison with the already-cited Pang et al. force-from-distance approach and adds references on straight-through estimation, numerical adjoints, and concurrent musculoskeletal MPC. The brown-noise citation changes from Eberhard et al. to Pinneri et al. The overall penalty-based simulation and contact-invariant optimization positioning remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and substantial method passages are rewritten. Solver equations and straight-through code move into the main text, while the former limitations section is reorganized into appendix tuning and limitations discussions. Section organization, author information, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds cube-reorientation and batching figures, condenses the existing integrator benchmark into Figure 5, and extensively rearranges illustrations. v1 Figure 1 becomes Figure 13, while Figure S7's renderings move to Figure 11. Plot styling, captions, figure grouping, and document layout are substantially revised.

improvement.justification: The implementation guidance in Appendices B/C.1 and new cube-control evidence improve usability and empirical support. Most integration and identification evidence already existed in v1, so the gains are incremental. The batching experiment establishes independent timestep choices rather than universally absent slowdowns, and some explicit identification caveats are lost; these temper the overall benefit.
